note: Forge-native unit names (metre, kilometre, inch, nautical-mile, astronomical-unit, light-year, and so on) instead of CyberChef's menu, with a source and a target unit. The sum is exact: every unit is an exact ratio of the metre (international yard of 1959, NIST SP 811), the value is decimal text with an optional sign and exponent, and the result is rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (20 by default, as CyberChef) and written in plain decimal form. The ratios agree with CyberChef's except the fathom and the nautical mile: CyberChef's fathom is 1.853184 m and its nautical mile 1,853.184 m, where the fathom is 6 feet (1.8288 m) and the nautical mile 1,852 m by definition. No parsec (it is not a rational number of metres), and none of the comparison units (cars, football fields). A value that is not a number is E_COERCE.

Same design as Convert distance: Forge-native unit names, exact ratios of the base unit, and the result rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (the digits parameter, 20 by default, as CyberChef's BigNumber rounds). Exact ratios of the square metre (the acre is 4046.8564224 m2); CyberChef's nuclear-physics and comparison units are not offered.

Same design as Convert distance: Forge-native unit names, exact ratios of the base unit, and the result rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (the digits parameter, 20 by default, as CyberChef's BigNumber rounds). Exact ratios of the kilogram (the international pound is 0.45359237 kg; the grain, carat and troy ounce are exact); the archaic and comparison units are not offered.

Same design as Convert distance: Forge-native unit names, exact ratios of the base unit, and the result rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (the digits parameter, 20 by default, as CyberChef's BigNumber rounds). Exact ratios of the metre per second (the knot is 1852 m per hour, the mile per hour 0.44704 m/s, kilometre per hour 1/3.6): CyberChef's factors are rounded (0.2778 m/s for a kilometre per hour, 1.6092 km/h for a mile per hour, a knot of 1.8517 km/h), so its results differ from the fourth digit. Mach is not offered, because it depends on the air, and neither are the comparison and scientific speeds.

Same design as Convert distance: Forge-native unit names, exact ratios of the base unit, and the result rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (the digits parameter, 20 by default, as CyberChef's BigNumber rounds). Bits, nibbles, bytes, the decimal units (kilo to exa, powers of 1000) and the binary units (kibi to exbi, IEC 80000-13, powers of 1024), as bits and as bytes. Equal to CyberChef's for the units both have, except that CyberChef rounds its conversion factors, so from the 17th digit on (petabyte or exabyte to exbibyte) its results are off; Forge has no deca-, hecto-, zetta- or yotta- units.

One op with a source format (auto detects it), a target format and a precision. Formats: decimal degrees, degrees and decimal minutes, degrees minutes and seconds, geohash, UTM and MGRS (WGS 84, 80 S to 84 N; Karney's series, sub-millimetre). Degrees convert exactly (whole numbers of 10^-12 degree). The Ordnance Survey National Grid is not offered: it needs the OSGB36 datum shift, which cannot be done exactly from a published formula. CyberChef's delimiter and direction menus are replaced by a reader that accepts any separator and the letters N S E W before or after the numbers; the output always writes the hemisphere letters (degrees notations) or a sign (decimal degrees). MGRS and geohash input is read as the middle of its cell.

The input is CyberChef's one line, lat1, lng1, lat2, lng2 in decimal degrees, or the two positions on two lines, each in any format that Convert co-ordinate format reads; the radius is a number in kilometres (6371 by default); the result is in metres, rounded to the millimetre, as decimal text (CyberChef prints the full floating-point number, the same to the millimetre).

file-mode:parse writes CyberChef's report: Textual representation, Octal representation, the File type line when a type character was given, the set-user-ID, set-group-ID and sticky bit lines, and the box with an X for each read, write and execute bit. It reads an octal mode of three or four digits (CyberChef also reads one or two, which it takes as the user and group digits), or symbolic text with or without the type character (CyberChef needs the type character). file-mode:convert only changes the notation (octal or symbolic).
The first 8 hex digits of the 24-digit ObjectID as seconds since the epoch, written as an ISO 8601 UTC time with a .000 fraction.

Reads hex (3, 4, 6 or 8 digits, with or without #), rgb()/rgba(), hsl()/hsla() and cmyk() and writes a text report of hex, RGB, RGBA, HSL, HSLA and CMYK with whole-number channels; CyberChef also draws a colour swatch, and Forge's ops return text. Colour names are not read.
